summary: Sulfadiazine is a short-acting systemic sulfonamide antibacterial that inhibits bacterial folate synthesis. It is used (often with pyrimethamine) for toxoplasmosis, for nocardiosis, as secondary prophylaxis of rheumatic fever in penicillin-allergic patients, and for some urinary tract and other susceptible infections. Adequate hydration and urine output are essential to prevent crystalluria and renal injury, and it can cause serious hypersensitivity skin reactions and blood dyscrasias.
indications: Toxoplasmosis (in combination with pyrimethamine and folinic acid)
Secondary prophylaxis of acute rheumatic fever in patients allergic to penicillin
Treatment of susceptible urinary tract and other systemic infections (including some meningococcal carriage / chancroid historically)

dosage.d: 1-1.5 g orally four times daily WITH pyrimethamine and folinic acid
Loading 2-4 g, then 2-4 g/day in 3-6 divided doses

dosage.n: With pyrimethamine for toxoplasmosis; not for infants <2 months

admin: Take with a full glass of water and maintain high fluid intake (urine output >1.2-1.5 L/day) to avoid crystalluria
Alkalinizing the urine reduces crystallization risk
For toxoplasmosis, give together with pyrimethamine and folinic acid to reduce hematologic toxicity
Avoid in late pregnancy and in neonates under 2 months
moa: Sulfadiazine is a structural analogue of para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA). It competitively inhibits dihydropteroate synthase, blocking bacterial synthesis of dihydrofolic acid and thereby of folate, purines and nucleic acids. Its action is bacteriostatic and synergistic with pyrimethamine (which blocks the next step, dihydrofolate reductase) in toxoplasmosis.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to sulfonamides (including sulfonamide diuretics, sulfonylureas)
Infants younger than 2 months (except in congenital toxoplasmosis under specialist care)

preg: Sulfonamides cross the placenta. They are best avoided near term and at delivery because of the risk of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia and kernicterus (displacement of bilirubin from albumin). Use earlier in pregnancy only when the benefit clearly outweighs the risk (e.g., toxoplasmosis treatment with appropriate folinic acid).
lact: Sulfonamides pass into breast milk. Avoid breastfeeding of jaundiced, premature, ill, or G6PD-deficient infants because of the risk of hyperbilirubinemia/kernicterus and hemolysis; otherwise use with caution.
renal: Use with caution and ensure good hydration and adequate urine output to prevent precipitation of the drug/its acetylated metabolite (crystalluria, hematuria, obstruction). Reduce the dose in renal impairment; alkalinization of urine helps.
hepatic: Use with caution; sulfonamides can cause hepatotoxicity. Avoid in severe hepatic impairment.

major: Methotrexate (displaced from protein and reduced clearance - toxicity)
minor: Para-aminobenzoic acid and procaine-type local anesthetics antagonize sulfonamide action
interactions.food: Take with plenty of fluid; no specific food restriction
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - increased GI and hepatic adverse effects
interactions.diagnostics: May cause false-positive urinary glucose (Benedict) and elevated creatinine/urine protein readings

serious: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)

monitoring: Renal function and urinalysis for crystalluria
Watch for early signs of rash or mucosal involvement (stop immediately)
counsel: Drink plenty of water throughout treatment to protect your kidneys
Stop the drug and seek care urgently if you develop a rash, blistering, mouth sores, fever, or sore throat
Use sun protection - the drug can make skin sensitive to sunlight
Tell your doctor if you have G6PD deficiency, kidney or liver problems, or are taking warfarin, methotrexate, or diabetes pills
pk: Absorbed within hours; bacteriostatic effect over the dosing interval
Plasma peak approximately 3-6 hours after an oral dose
Store at room temperature, protected from light and moisture
pearls: Workhorse partner of pyrimethamine for toxoplasmosis - always give folinic acid to limit marrow toxicity
Crystalluria is preventable with high fluid intake and urine alkalinization
Avoid at term and in young infants because of bilirubin displacement and kernicterus risk

NOTE: oral systemic sulfadiazine is no longer an FDA-listed product in the US; dosing here follows the WHO/BNF and the established sulfonamide class prescribing information - confirm against local formulary
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember with a full glass of water. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip it - do not double up. Try to keep doses evenly spaced.
overdose: Overdose may cause nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dizziness, drowsiness, and, with large amounts, crystalluria, hematuria, anuria, and blood dyscrasias. Management is supportive: force fluids, alkalinize the urine, monitor blood counts and renal function. Hemodialysis can remove the drug in severe cases.
